Edit : Fixed typo
Perhaps try a collection of smaller stories. They are easier to get through and can be a part of a story arc so it's not something new every 20 pages.

On that point, OP, I just finished 'There's Something I Want You To Do' by Charles Baxter and, for my money, each story is as engaging as the last, with recurring characters and events that link them all together in a loose sort of web. I found it a lovely, heartfelt study in human moments and personal morality, well within the themes of 1Q84 but in more bite-sized chunks.

It's certainly not a 'feel-good' book, but it's emotionally challenging and every story has a different tone that, personally, I couldn't put down.

If you find that kind of thing enjoyable, the draw to pick the book back up could be a boon to your time-management. Whenever I'm grumpy about not having time to read, I look at how I spend my down-time otherwise and am often surprised at how much fat there is to trim when what I have to do is give up sitting around while waiting for water to boil (or doing laundry, or having a 2, etc.)

This might be both contentious and subjective, but I wonder who in the world of journalism I should pay attention to.

This voat thread made me think about journalists and their individual integrity versus the papers they write for. I admit that I would at first glance think that The Sunday Times (who published bullshyt in this instance) have more credibility than The Intercept (until I read their about page, I had not heard the name before today. One of 10000 or whatever).

It seems that personal integrity is becoming more important than institutional integrity. People change jobs and affiliations, and institutions too. I would and should trust a piece on a minor website that is confirmed to be from a reputable journalist more than a maintream source with a new or disreputable writer.

So my question is: as of today, who still have integrity as journalists? Who have over a period of years proven over and over again that they are trustworthy, have an ability to get in touch with important sources, do not exaggerate/lie, are not in the pocket of politicians or powerful people, but still keep churning out articles?

Glenn Greenwald is on my list and triggered the question, so is someone like Robert Fisk. But I have to admit that I look at the domain name more than the byline, and I'd like that to change.

Super bonus points for pointing out journalists you usually disagree with. Who is the most trustworthy right-wing journalist that I should read to get a fair but balanced view?
None of them. As long as journalists are in bed with advertisers, there are no credible journalists. The best you can do is take from all sources with their bias in mind, and form your own opinions.

The main "journalist" I would say that is really fair and balanced would be Sharyl Attkisson. She's a pretty equal opportunity hitter. She used to be someone that the left used to triumph as fair until the allegations emerged of her being hacked by the feds (still hasn't been proven, but given that same thing happening to other reporters...).

I think when you think of journalist, you're also bunching in opinion writers. I could be prickly and say how the two are separate, but I won't. Some good right-wing opinion writers to seek out are Thomas Sowell (one of the most brilliant men in recent history IMHO), George Will, and Charles Krauthammer.
